extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalists, communication researchers, and policymakers interested in news coverage of climate science
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating or producing news coverage of climate change (and similar science-policy topics) with attention to journalistic norms that shape story selection and construction and how those norms can bias representation of scientific consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Story focus on individual figures (politicians, activists, scientists) rather than aggregate evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personalization privileges individual voices and allows selection of contrarian individuals to 'balance' mainstream consensus; operationally, stories that include a prominent individual scientist quote outrank stories that present institutional or aggregate consensus statements. Anti-pattern: framing science as a set of competing people rather than evaluated bodies of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatization
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasis on conflict, urgency, dramatic visuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatization produces a premium for conflict-based narratives and can manufacture controversy by forcing a two-sided dramatic frame even when science is settled. Conflict-hook premium: stories pegged to disputes receive more coverage than steady-state findings. Avoid prioritizing spectacle over representativeness of the evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for new, surprising findings over repetition of established consensus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty causes cherry-picking of studies that appear to challenge consensus; confirmation of consensus is rarely newsworthy while challenges receive disproportionate attention. Operational 'novelty threshold' means routine confirmation is deprioritized. Journalists should be cautious equating 'new' with 'contradictory' without methodological evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority-Order
rubrics_metrics.description: Citing authoritative sources with an internal hierarchy (government > scientists > NGOs > activists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This source-hierarchy shapes who gets quoted and trusted; when personalization is high, contrarian individuals can be elevated within this hierarchy, leading to misuse of authority. Guidance: evaluate authority in terms of relevant expertise and consensus rather than positional or institutional status alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting 'both sides' of contested topics (equal-time or roughly equal attention to opposing positions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When scientific consensus is heavily lopsided, equal-time balance misrepresents the state of knowledge ('balance-as-bias'). Example empirical finding: over a 15-year period 52.7% of prestige-press articles gave 'roughly equal attention' to pro-anthropogenic and pro-natural-variation positions despite ~95%+ scientific consensus for anthropogenic warming. Avoid applying symmetry of airtime where asymmetry of evidence exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-Sided Framing Premium
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories admitting clean two-sided framing are favored over nuanced consensus-with-caveats reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This operational selection bias rewards narratives that can be simplified into two opposed camps. Consequence: complex, probabilistic, or caveated consensus reporting is deprioritized. Reporters/editors should prefer frames that reflect degrees of evidence rather than forced binary oppositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict-Hook Premium
rubrics_metrics.description: Climate stories pegged to disputes (between scientists, policy actors, advocacy groups) are covered more than steady-state findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because news values prize conflict, coverage concentrates on disputes even when they are marginal to the underlying science. Guidance: assess newsworthiness against representativeness of the scientific community, not merely existence of disagreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalized Scientist Quote (operational selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories citing prominent individual scientists outrank stories presenting institutional consensus statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This amplifies personalization and can allow outlier voices to be treated as equivalent to consensus. Alternative practice: give proportional weight to consensus statements (e.g., IPCC, major expert surveys) and contextualize individual quotes within the broader evidence base.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis-Event Pegging
rubrics_metrics.description: Climate receives coverage when extreme weather or crisis events provide a 'hook'; baseline trend coverage is thin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Event-driven coverage emphasizes episodic links rather than long-term trend reporting, leading to undercoverage of gradual but important changes. Editorial guidance: include routine trend and consensus-context pieces, not just event-linked reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty Threshold (operational)
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirmation of consensus is rarely newsworthy; challenges to consensus are disproportionately newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically, newsrooms prioritize studies or claims that appear to contradict mainstream views. This creates selection bias; validate novelty claims by examining methodological robustness and relation to cumulative evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance-as-Bias / Equal-Time Misrepresentation (empirical finding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Equal-attention balance reporting can quantitatively misrepresent scientific consensus when one position is overwhelmingly supported by experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boykoff's core empirical result: media 'balance' produced coverage statistically divergent from scientific consensus (1990–2002). Use empirical benchmarks (e.g., expert surveys, IPCC) to detect and quantify such misrepresentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalizability: Benchmarking Against Scientific Consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage can be benchmarked against scientific consensus indexes (IPCC reports, expert surveys); deviation measures quantify 'balance-as-bias'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply explicit benchmarks to evaluate representativeness (e.g., proportion of articles giving attention proportional to expert agreement). This provides a measurable standard for assessing newsworthiness and bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic Amplification of Norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Online news selection often inherits journalistic norms and can amplify them via algorithmic engagement weights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithmic prioritization (clicks, shares) may magnify personalization, dramatization, and novelty premiums. Newsroom and platform designers should consider how engagement metrics interact with professional norms and adjust signals to favor accurate representation of consensus where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive Applicability to Other Consensus-vs-Contrarian Topics
rubrics_metrics.description: The same norms and biases that operate in climate coverage are expected to predict coverage patterns for vaccines, evolution, GMO safety, masking, and similar topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing or producing coverage of other science-policy issues, apply the same diagnostics (personalization, balance, novelty, conflict hooks) and benchmark against domain-specific consensus to detect analogous balance-as-bias dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Norms Can Systematically Distort Coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Individually defensible professional norms (balance, personalization, dramatization, novelty) can jointly produce structural misinformation on settled-science topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial evaluation should consider systemic interactions of norms, not just adherence to single professional rules. Anti-pattern: defending a practice solely because it aligns with a single journalistic norm without checking aggregate effect on representativeness.
